name: Gitksan
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Brown, Jason, Henry Davis, Michael Schwan & Barbara Sennott. 2016. Gitksan. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 46(3): 367-378. doi:10.1017/S0025100315000432 (open access, Cambridge Core)
catalog_locator: p. 373, section 'Stress' (of the Cambridge Core PDF)
catalog_quote: Rigsby (1986: 213–217) is responsible for the primary observations on Gitksan stress. He notes that in lexical words (verbs, nouns, and adjectives), stress falls on the rightmost vowel of the root. Examples include [ɢaˈniːs] ‘dog salmon’ /qəniːs/ and [ˈlaːɢaldiˀj] ‘I examined it’ /laːq-əl-tə-ˀj/ (examine-?-T-1SG.II) (Rigsby 1986: 213). In compounds stress is found on the rightmost root-vowel of the rightmost member of the compound. In contrast, in preverbs, which have some lexical content, stress is on the leftmost vowel. Phrasal stress in Gitksan falls on the rightmost root-vowel of the head word. Suffixes are invisible to stress assignment (Rigsby 1986: 216 notes only two exceptions).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is morphologically bounded: in lexical words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) it falls on the rightmost vowel of the root, i.e. the last root syllable, and suffixes (and the transitive vowel, pronominal enclitics etc.) are ignored, so a suffixed word such as /laːq-əl-tə-ˀj/ is stressed on the root vowel [ˈlaːɢaldiˀj]. Compounds stress the rightmost root vowel of the final member; preverbs (a closed adverb-like class) are stressed on their leftmost vowel and do not carry primary stress in the phrase. Hunt 1993: 232 fn. 51 states the same rule independently ('suffixes are never stressed. The stress is normally on the last (long) vowel of the root'). Roots are mostly monosyllabic, so the pattern is often indistinguishable from root-final stress; secondary marking [ˌboʁaˈbaʁa] appears in a reduplicated form (p. 372) but no secondary-stress rule is stated.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; a transcription [ˌboʁaˈbaʁa] on p. 372 shows a secondary mark on a reduplicant, but no rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Suffixes are invisible to stress 'with only two exceptions' (Rigsby 1986: 216, not named in the JIPA text); Hunt 1993: 232 fn. 51 likewise excepts 'a few non-productive derivational suffixes'. Preverbs/prenominals are a separate class stressed on their leftmost vowel and lacking phrasal primary stress (Hunt 1993: 21).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (root within the morphological word); the text also states phrasal stress (rightmost root-vowel of the head word). Data from two Eastern Gitksan (Kispiox) speakers; the stress statement itself is Rigsby's 1986 description of Gitksan generally.
new_statements.identity_note: The JIPA Illustration describes Eastern Gitksan (Kispiox/Glen Vowell/Hazelton) as spoken by two sisters from Kispiox; the stress statement is Rigsby's 1986 description of Gitksan in general (Rigsby worked mainly with Western/Kitsegukla and other villages). Glottolog treats Gitxsan as a single language gitx1241 (ISO git); the Eastern/Western split is dialectal (vowel shift, stop lenition), not reported to affect stress.

new_statements.quote: 2.1.2.3. Stress In this presentation I have only indicated stress as being either primary, /´/, or secondary, /`/. Rigsby has pointed out that only heads of phrases and the second members of compounds receive primary stress and that all other adverbial and adnominal elements are proclitic and unstressed⁵. ⁵ This information was obtained from Rigsby, 1970.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's root-final (morphological) placement from Rigsby 1986 via Brown et al. 2016 and Hunt 1993, but silent on word-internal placement; it adds only the phrasal domain (heads of phrases / second member of compounds stressed, proclitics unstressed), which matches Hunt 1993's remark that preverbals lack primary stress. Nothing contradicts the catalog. Access note: the listed open_url is a dead ANLA legacy page; the scan was downloaded fromhttps://uafanlc.alaska.edu/Online/TS971W1974/TS971W1974.pdf(118 MB, no text), 33 pages scanned, extract kept, source PDF deleted per the big-file rule; the stress passage was verified against the page scan.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The thesis only marks primary (acute) and secondary (grave) stress on its transcriptions and, citing Rigsby 1970, states a phrasal distribution: primary stress goes to the head of a phrase and to the second member of a compound; preposed adverbial and adnominal elements are proclitic and unstressed. It gives no rule for where stress falls within a word or root, no weight statement; the distribution section (syllable types, onsets, codas, pp. 44-49) and the vowel-allophone section (pp. 39-41) never mention stress, and the author says the study is primarily about segmental phonemes (p. 11).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress exists only as a notational category (grave accent); no rule for its placement is given.
new_statements.exceptions: None; only that proclitic adverbial/adnominal elements are unstressed and second members of compounds carry the primary stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Wickstrom's data are from Hazelton (principal consultant Mrs. Sarah Marshall), with additional speakers from Kitwanga, Skeena Crossing and Kispiox; he treats these together as Gitksan (his 'Nass-Gitksan' groups Gitksan with Nisga'a following Rigsby, but the thesis describes Gitksan only).
